analysis.one_liner: Gives state and local government workers federal collective bargaining rights when their state denies them.
analysis.headline: With 204 cosponsors, the bill never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: About half the states either bar public employees from bargaining or cover only some of them. This bill would require the Federal Labor Relations Authority to check each state's laws against a federal floor of bargaining rights, and in states that fall short, the Authority would run union elections and enforce bargaining rules itself. States with adequate laws would keep their own systems untouched. The bill also bans strikes and lockouts that would disrupt emergency or public safety services.
analysis.who_benefits: Public employees — teachers, nurses, EMTs, corrections workers, and others — in states that do not substantially protect collective bargaining. They would gain the right to organize, elect a union, bargain over wages and working conditions, and enforce those contracts through binding arbitration or the Federal Labor Relations Authority. Supervisory employees are included, and unions would gain dues-paying members in states that currently bar bargaining.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public workers in states without bargaining rights

how_it_helps.text: The Federal Labor Relations Authority must determine, within 180 days, whether each state's laws substantially provide a federal minimum of bargaining rights, including the right to organize, form or join a union, and bargain collectively [S2][S3].

In states that fall short, the Authority must issue rules and administer union elections, unit determinations, complaint hearings, and binding impasse resolution; states with adequate laws keep their own systems [S2][S3].
Workers and unions could enforce rights through the Authority, and after a charge sits unresolved, through a federal lawsuit with attorney's fees available [S3].
Public employers must recognize a union chosen by a majority vote and put any agreement in writing, and union dues could be paid through payroll deduction [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments would bear higher labor costs if workers in currently non-bargaining states win contracts, and those costs land on taxpayers. States would also lose some control over how their public workforce is organized. Emergency and law enforcement workers would give up the ability to strike, though most states already prohibit that.

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state labor law: any state the Authority finds lacking would have its bargaining rules for covered employees administered by a federal agency, and small towns could be exempted from state bargaining laws only by opting out before the determination [S3].

Public sector bargaining is expensive for governments — higher wages, benefits, and pension discussions add to state and local budgets, and the bill authorizes whatever appropriations are needed to run the new federal system [S3].

The bill excludes management, confidential, and elected officials from coverage, allows states not to require bargaining over pensions, and bars any strike, lockout, or job action likely to disrupt emergency or public safety services, so some workers gain less than the bill's title suggests [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of public employees in states that bar or narrow bargaining, the bill offered a real, enforceable right they otherwise lack, with emergency services protected by an explicit strike ban. The cost is genuine but bounded: government labor costs rise where bargaining is new, and states give up part of their authority over workforce rules. The design largely preserves state systems that already work, which limits the federal footprint. The main honest objection is the federal override of state choices on a matter states have historically controlled.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced the bill on October 26, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S1][S5].
It gathered 204 cosponsors — 200 Democrats and 4 Republicans — but the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action [S4][S5].
The CRS summary describes the bill as providing minimum collective bargaining rights for public employees while prohibiting strikes by certain public safety workers [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public employers in states that restrict bargaining, who keep the status quo: no federal bargaining floor was imposed, and no new union rights were created. Public workers in those states remain without enforceable bargaining rights.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 200 of the 204 cosponsors were Democrats, with only 4 Republicans — and the House Democratic committee chair who controlled the bill's schedule never moved it.

industries.note: In states that bar or restrict bargaining, the bill would create union members and dues streams the unions currently cannot access, while giving those workers an enforceable right to bargain. Workers' gain and the unions' gain run in the same direction here.

Governments in restrictive states would face union elections, binding contracts, and potentially higher wage and benefit costs, which fall ultimately on local taxpayers. Governments that already provide adequate rights would be left alone.

Public employers found to have interfered with organizing could face compliance orders and federal lawsuits with attorney's fees, removing the practical inability to enforce that workers face in non-bargaining states.
